W7213591576.abstract: Language-model agents are increasingly asked to carry out work spanning days or weeks, such as an operations remediation or a research programme. Such a task outlives any context window, any process and any interval at which a person can attend. In this paper, we argue that a long-horizon agent must run continually without forgetting before it can learn continually. This ability lies in the harness around the model rather than in the model itself. We derive seven bottlenecks from the long-horizon setting and answer them with a hierarchical architecture of three parts: (i) levels indexed by time scale, each keeping a bounded file summarising the level below; (ii) a clocked tick as the unit of autonomous action; and (iii) cascaded intelligence, where work is escalated to a more capable model only after failing review. We report on a ten-day campaign in which an agent built on this architecture reproduced a published reinforcement-learning result with a human attending once a day, and show (1) the agent kept the thread across every context reset and session boundary of the campaign, (2) operating knowledge written early changed later behaviour with no change to model weights, and (3) where learned components would enter such a system. Overall, our experience suggests continual learning for these agents needs a substrate outliving every context and process, and the checks the harness already runs are where a learner belongs.

W7213966365.abstract: Machine translation, as a core approach in natural language processing, plays a crucial role in promoting cross-lingual communication. This study proposes an English-to-target language translation model that integrates enhanced back-translation with translation memory, aiming to address the issues of low training efficiency, slow convergence, and weak domain adaptability in traditional machine translation models for English-to-multilingual tasks. The model accelerates translation training from English to the target language through enhanced back-translation and leverages translation memory to enhance the capture of specialized terminology and domain knowledge. Experimental results show that the proposed model reaches a loss function value of 0.060 at the final iteration, achieving an accuracy of 85.55% and an F1 score of 84.60%. In translation performance tests, the model achieves BLEU scores of 55.10, 51.47, 59.33, and 54.22 on four domain-specific datasets, all substantially higher than those of the comparative models. Case studies involving Russian, German, and French translations, along with heatmap visualization, further confirm its strengths in terminology accuracy and cross-lingual alignment. The innovation of this research lies in effectively integrating back-translation optimization with translation memory, significantly enhancing the efficiency, accuracy, and domain adaptability of machine translation. This provides a novel solution for high-performance and practical English-source language translation systems.

W7214026869.abstract: Introduction and Purpose The increasing contribution of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) to hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) has highlighted important limitations of conventional ultrasound-based surveillance. Obesity, hepatic steatosis, and heterogeneous liver parenchyma may impair visualization and reduce sensitivity for early-stage tumors. This review summarizes current evidence on HCC risk stratification, surveillance, diagnosis, and treatment, with particular emphasis on risk-adapted strategies in patients with MASLD. Materials and Methods Peer-reviewed literature was reviewed, with emphasis on studies addressing ultrasound-based surveillance, abbreviated magnetic resonance imaging (AMRI), elastography, biomarker-based risk models, liquid biopsy, radiomics, artificial intelligence, and recent advances in locoregional and systemic treatment. Results Ultrasound with or without alpha-fetoprotein remains the standard surveillance strategy for patients at increased risk of HCC, although its effectiveness is reduced when visualization is inadequate. In selected patients, alternative imaging approaches, including AMRI, may improve surveillance performance. Elastography, clinical risk models, and biomarker panels such as GALAD may support risk stratification, whereas liquid biopsy, radiomics, and artificial intelligence remain investigational. Advances in locoregional therapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy have also expanded treatment options across different stages of HCC. Conclusion The key challenge is to identify patients in whom ultrasound-based surveillance is insufficient rather than to replace ultrasonography universally. A risk-adapted strategy integrating individual HCC risk, ultrasound quality, and selected complementary tools may be particularly relevant in MASLD. Further prospective studies are needed to determine whether such approaches improve early detection and clinical outcomes.

W7214095351.abstract: Software-defined vehicles (SDVs) are transforming automotive systems by shifting vehicle functionality from predominantly hardware-centric implementations toward software-intensive, continuously evolving platforms.This transition introduces substantial challenges for validation because vehicle behavior increasingly depends on distributed software components, connected services, electronic control units, sensors, communication networks, and frequently updated software releases.Conventional validation approaches, which rely heavily on manually designed test cases and predefined execution workflows, can become difficult to scale across the growing combinations of software configurations, operating conditions, and vehicle scenarios.Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) provides an emerging approach for addressing these limitations by enabling autonomous software agents to plan validation activities, generate test scenarios, execute experiments, analyze outcomes, identify anomalous behavior, and iteratively refine subsequent validation tasks.This article presents a generalized framework for applying agentic AI to autonomous validation of SDV platforms.The proposed approach considers interactions among agentic reasoning components, simulation environments, digital representations of vehicle systems, automated test-generation mechanisms, observability platforms, and continuous integration and delivery pipelines.The Agentic AI Frameworks for Autonomous Validation of Software-Defined Vehicle Platforms https://iaeme.com/Home/journal/IJCET33

W7214155520.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agents to tackle long-horizon tasks across diverse environments. To further improve agent performance, existing language world models typically predict environment observations, yet reconstructing high-entropy, execution-dependent tool responses offers limited value when real feedback is available. Meanwhile, agents suffer from \emph{task-state contamination}, where unsupported assumptions and outdated plans persist in history and distort subsequent decisions. We propose the \textbf{Agent-Editing World Model (AEWM)}, which models how reasoning and actions shape future task progress rather than simulating tool responses. AEWM combines \textbf{Action Judge} to distinguish \textsc{Critical}, \textsc{Exploratory}, and \textsc{Noisy} decisions with \textbf{State Revision} to edit noisy reasoning--action continuations from the same observed history. \textbf{EditAct} integrates these capabilities with real execution, directly changing the state underlying subsequent decisions rather than merely providing critiques. We train AEWM across Search, Terminal, and Software Engineering through mid-training and supervised fine-tuning. AEWM achieves 70.5\% macro-F1 on our Action Judge benchmark, exceeding the strongest frontier baseline by 10.6 points. Across six benchmarks and three agent backbones, EditAct improves average scores by 3.2--6.7 points over the strongest baseline. Furthermore, rejection sampling fine-tuning on verified EditAct trajectories, termed \textbf{AEWM-RFT}, improves over Self-RFT by 2.2--2.6 points across three domains without online AEWM guidance.

W7214316330.abstract: The rapid progression of large language models is extending AI from passive content generation into the active workflows of engineering and scientific discovery. This shift raises a compelling question: can AI be both the object of development and an active participant in building next-generation AI systems? We explore this question by building Qwen-Planner-Agent within a closed-loop AI-for-AI framework for scalable development and iterative improvement. Mobile planning offers a demanding test of this approach: complex, long-horizon tasks challenge agent reliability, while costly real-device interaction limits development scalability. The framework connects data production, model training, and deployment through a shared action-feedback-verification contract. (i) AI for Data builds a human-gated agentic data flywheel in which specialized agents construct tasks, collect interaction trajectories, curate and balance training data, and use training feedback to guide subsequent data generation. (ii) AI for Training combines a supervised planning cold start with hybrid-environment online agentic reinforcement learning, where we introduce Competence-Aware Reward-and-Advantage Engineering (CARE) to reduce reasoning and tool-use costs while preserving task performance. (iii) AI drives model--harness co-evolution through an execution-evidence-driven loop that orchestrates memory, skills, and tools at runtime and feeds structured action feedback and preserved failure traces back into coordinated model and harness adaptation. Qwen-Planner-Agent achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated models and systems on MobilePA-Bench, improving over its base model across tool use, memory, skills, and sub-agent coordination. Further evaluations of our model show improvements across non-mobile agentic benchmarks while largely preserving general capabilities.

W7214381949.abstract: Abstract Deep learning for three dimension (3D) modalities such as CT, MRI, and PET offers promise to improve diagnostic accuracy, surgical planning, and visualization of disease progression, as 3D image data provide high resolution volumetric representation. However, 3D deep learning models are computationally heavy and demand powerful hardware that is not always available or affordable, restrictingtheir use in resource-constrained settings such as rural clinics, edge devices, and low- and middle-income countries. Hence, there is a growing interest in building lightweight deep learning models, in general, and for 3D imaging, in particular. This article systematically and critically reviews lightweight deep learning for processing 3D medical images, examining model compression techniques such as knowledge distillation, quantization, pruning and efficient architectural designs, together with the datasets, tools, and deployment environments involved. These techniques substantially reduce parameters, memory, and inference time with modest accuracy loss. We also identify several research gaps in these approaches, such as the accuracy mismatch between lightweight and standard models, difficulty handling small anatomical structures while keeping models compact, limited testing on real resource-constrained hardware, weak integration of clinical information, and the absence of efficiency-aware evaluation metrics. We outline future directions, cluding robust lightweight designs, purpose-built compact 3D datasets, standardized efficiency metrics, and lightweight multimodal models.

W7214556581.abstract: The field of artificial intelligence is currently navigating a profound transition from the paradigm of static, predictive language modeling to that of dynamic, agentic reasoning. This shift reframes Large Language Models (LLMs) not merely as engines for stochastic sequence generation but as the cognitive cores of autonomous agents capable of perception, planning, action execution, and continual self-improvement. This survey provides an exhaustive and rigorous analysis of the agentic reasoning landscape, organizing the domain into a three-layered taxonomy: Foundational Agentic Reasoning, which establishes core single-agent capabilities such as planning, tool use, and search; Self-Evolving Agentic Reasoning, which examines mechanisms for feedback integration, memory persistence, and lifelong adaptation; and Collective Multi-Agent Reasoning, which explores the emergent intelligence of coordinated agent systems. Across these layers, we critically evaluate the dichotomy between in-context reasoning (inference-time orchestration without parameter updates) and post-training reasoning (reinforcement learning, supervised fine-tuning, and policy optimization). We further synthesize insights from recent benchmarks (e.g., GAIA, SWE-bench, ALFWorld) and real-world applications to assess the current state of the art. W7214625715.abstract: BACKGROUND: Approximately 30% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA) do not respond to tocilizumab (TCZ). This study aimed to predict TCZ response using machine learning models trained on clinical data. METHODS: Baseline and follow-up data from patients with RA treated with TCZ were collected. Seven different machine learning models (logistic regression, K-nearest neighbor algorithm, random forest, support vector machine, decision tree, gradient boosting, and boosting algorithm) were trained to predict the treatment response of patients with RA across different imaging stages after three to six months of therapy. The area under the receiver operating curve (AUC) was the main performance evaluation feature to screen the best model, and the relative importance of each variable in the model was ranked using the Shapley Additive Explanation (SHAP) value. RESULTS: A total of 245 RA patients treated with TCZ were included. The logistic regression model demonstrated superior prediction performance across imaging stages, achieving AUC scores of 0.78 for patients without imaging changes, 0.73 for stage I, and 0.82 for stages II, III, and IV. Key features influencing predictions varied by imaging stage. The most important features were D-dimer concentration for patients without imaging changes, DAS28 grade for patients in stage I, and the physician's overall disease score (EGA) for patients in stages II, III, and IV, with SHAP values of 0.5180, 0.6661, and 1.3978, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates the potential of machine learning to predict TCZ treatment outcomes and identify stage-specific features in patients with RA. CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.

W7214786648.abstract: Two complementary technological routes, smart renewable–hydrogen energy networks and fusion-assisted electricity generation, are of great interest in the global push towards decarbonised power systems. Renewable-Hydrogen networks combine variable renewables (such as solar, wind, and hydro) and electrolysis with delivery, storage, and digital management to provide dispatchable, carbon-free electricity. Meanwhile, after recent strides in ignition and with rising private-sector funding, fusion energy is becoming a long-term, high-density, low-carbon alternative to renewable-hydrogen generation. This review compiles recent literature (2020-2025) on the various production methods for green hydrogen, hydrogen storage technologies, smart grid management with the aid of artificial intelligence, and the status of magnetic and inertial confinement fusion, before exploring the possibility of using fusion-assisted heat and electricity generation in conjunction with renewable hydrogen infrastructure for augmenting the reliability of the grid and minimising emissions throughout the hydrogen value chain. Three comparative tables summarise hydrogen production routes, hydrogen storage options, and fusion confinement approaches, and four proposed schematic figures visualise network architecture, production growth trends, fusion reactor concepts, and an integrated fusion–hydrogen– renewable smart grid. The paper discusses key barriers (capital cost, materials durability, electrolyser degradation, fusion engineering readiness, etc.) and the policy and research priorities needed to support a resilient, low-carbon electricity future.

W7214890125.abstract: Gradient-based reward guidance provides a flexible way to use downstream reward models to control masked diffusion language models at inference time. However, its computational cost remains high as each decoding iteration incurs expensive diffusion model forward passes and reward model backpropagation steps. To address this, we introduce FastGuide, an adaptive hybrid of parallel and autoregressive decoding to accelerate reward guidance for diffusion language models. In analogy to parallel decoding, FastGuide amortizes the cost of reward model backpropagation by computing guidance once per decoding step and reusing it to generate multiple tokens. Within each decoding step, FastGuide makes diffusion forward passes autoregressive by unmasking tokens one at a time while efficiently recomputing token distributions after each unmasking by utilizing KV caching techniques and sparse recomputation of attention. Lastly, to adapt hybrid decoding to the model's confidence, FastGuide defers any token that the model is unconfident about under its recomputed distribution. Experiments on three reward benchmarks demonstrate that FastGuide is up to $4.4\times$ faster than sequential reward-guided decoding while retaining similar generation quality.

W7214989179.abstract: The article is devoted to the urgent problem of using cognitive technologies, in particular artificial intelligence (AI), for monitoring and analyzing pharmaceutical markets. In the context of sanctions pressure and the need to reorient Russian non-energy exports, pharmaceuticals is considered one of the key high-tech industries. The author conducts a critical analysis of traditional methods of strategic marketing (SWOT analysis, Porter’s Five Forces model, BCG matrix, and Uppsala model). The analysis showed that traditional methods retain their theoretical value but demonstrate fundamental limitations in the modern economy; in the context of digitalization, these methods require integration with cognitive technologies to increase their accuracy, objectivity, and efficiency. The study revealed the significant potential of cognitive technologies (AI agents, LLM) to transform the monitoring processes of pharmaceutical markets. Based on the conducted research, an innovative concept of international strategic marketing based on the use of a multi-agent system was developed. The paper presents the concept of a multi-agent system architecture, where each specialized agent is responsible for a specific stage of analysis, from the initial clustering of markets and assessment of the competitive environment to the construction of optimal expansion routes. Special attention is paid to the comparison of capabilities of LLM and AI agents, as well as the analysis of advantages and risks of implementing cognitive systems. It is concluded that the symbiosis of AI capabilities for data processing and human expert assessment for final decision-making is the most effective strategy when entering new pharmaceutical markets, taking into account the risks of a lack of real understanding of the situation by cognitive systems.

W7215050241.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence is transforming online information environments, amplifying both societal benefits and risks. This article argues that online platforms can be understood as multi‐agent systems (MAS) composed of humans, simulated users, adversarial agents, and defensive agents operating under platform‐level rules. In this MAS‐based framework, persuasion, trust, coordination, and governance interact to shape system‐level outcomes. To study these dynamics safely, we introduce a sandbox environment in which human participants, red bots, green bots, and blue bots can be observed under controlled conditions. Early experiences with the sandbox show that persuasive agents can be built with little effort, that current large language model (LLM) agents lack psychological realism, and that humans may struggle to distinguish malicious red bots from benign participants. The sandbox enables stakeholders to experience and evaluate trade‐offs in moderation, amplification, and intervention strategies. We outline a research agenda for improving agent validity, modelling advanced threats, and designing human–machine teams that support healthier, more resilient information environments.

W7215054453.abstract: Road damage detection is essential for supporting efficient road infrastructure inspection, yet conventional visual assessment is time-consuming and may produce inconsistent results when dealing with diverse pavement distress patterns. This study aims to comparatively evaluate YOLOv8s, YOLOv10s, YOLOv11s, and an optimized YOLOv11s configuration for detecting and classifying longitudinal cracks, transverse cracks, alligator cracks, and potholes using the RDD2022 dataset. A quantitative experimental approach was employed using 55,007 annotated damage instances, with all models trained under consistent experimental conditions and evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, mAP@50, mAP@50–95, and inference time. The results show a progressive improvement across the evaluated configurations, with optimized YOLOv11s achieving the highest performance at 83.4% precision, 80.9% recall, 82.1% F1-score, 88.4% mAP@50, and 59.6% mAP@50–95, with an inference time of 8.7 ms. Class-specific analysis showed that longitudinal cracks achieved the highest F1-score of 85.5%, whereas alligator cracks recorded the lowest at 79.7%, with the largest classification confusion occurring between potholes and alligator cracks. The novelty of this study lies in the systematic cross-generation comparison of YOLOv8s, YOLOv10s, YOLOv11s, and optimized YOLOv11s under consistent experimental conditions while jointly examining overall performance, class-specific behavior, classification errors, and inference efficiency. The study contributes a detailed characterization of model performance across heterogeneous road-damage categories and provides quantitative evidence for selecting an effective YOLO configuration for automated road infrastructure inspection.

W7215098945.abstract: Scientific artificial intelligence (AI), spanning foundation models (FMs) to federated data-analysis pipelines, is becoming shared infrastructure across national laboratories, universities, hospitals, and industrial partners. This collaboration creates privacy risks whose natural unit is often an institution's participation, research strategy, or technical capability rather than a single record. Differential privacy (DP), federated learning (FL), secure computation, trusted execution, and provenance each protect parts of the stack, but their guarantees rarely compose across mixed-trust institutions, access tiers, and autonomous agents. This perspective recasts privacy for scientific AI as an assurance problem defined by six elements: protected asset, observer, channel, permitted disclosure, guarantee, and evidence. We demonstrate the framing through a claim register for a composite cross-institutional scenario and use it to assess the model lifecycle. Two of the resulting gaps are specific to leadership-class facilities: scheduler, allocation, and telemetry metadata expose an institution's resource posture, and instrument-attached control loops leak research strategy through timing and contention on shared accelerators. We identify six research priorities: institution-level guarantees, agent-communication privacy, cross-tier information flow, privacy-compatible reproducibility, leadership-scale accounting, and instrument side channels. The contribution is a common form for stating, comparing, and auditing claims whose guarantees otherwise remain fragmented across the scientific AI stack.

W7215124884.abstract: The telecommunications and enterprise sectors in Saudi Arabia are progressing from digitally based service operations towards more autonomous operating models in which artificial intelligence is able to understand objectives, identify situations, coordinate tools, and carry out specific actions. This report looks at the way in which AI agents can help to achieve autonomous service delivery in both telecom and enterprise operations while at the same time meeting the requirements relating to reliability, governance, cybersecurity, and human accountability that are linked to Saudi Vision 2030. The study makes use of a structured integrative review of peer-reviewed literature published between 2020 and 2025, with a focus on agentic AI, zero-touch network and service management, intent-based networking, AIOps, service operations, AI governance, human oversight, and Saudi digital transformation. The analysis highlights five interdependent capabilities: context-aware intent interpretation, multi-source observability, agentic reasoning and orchestration, closed-loop execution, and governance-by-design. It is shown that autonomy is most believable when it is implemented as bounded, observable, and reversible automation rather than as unrestricted machine control. Research in the telecom field has developed well-established foundations in the areas of intent life cycles, assurance, closed loops, and zero-touch management, whereas research relating to enterprise services brings in aspects such as incident intelligence, workflow enhancement, and service quality. The review introduces an Agentic Autonomous Service Delivery Framework that combines operational agents with policy constraints, confidence thresholds, digital audit trails, human escalation, and continuous assurance. This framework provides a practical research programme for Saudi organisations that wish to establish resilient, scalable, and trustworthy AI-enabled service operations in line with Vision 2030.

W7216193701.abstract: Arabic handwriting recognition (AHR) remains challenging due to the context-dependent, cursive script that’s affected by diacritic marks, overlapping strokes, and high writer variability. This review presents an overview of deep learning approaches for AHR in both online and offline settings. The literature search was carried out using IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, and Google Scholar, after screening titles, abstracts and reviewing the text of relevant studies, and the focused set were included. The most selected articles which meet the criteria were published between January 2015 and January 2026, in addition, one of the early articles which published on 2010 was included because it is representing the foundation for subsequent researches in this filed. This review covers recognition pipelines, and used datasets such as Arabic Handwritten Characters Dataset (AHCD), Institut für Nachrichtentechnik/ Ecole Nationale d'Ingénieurs de Tunis (IFN/ENIT), KHATT Handwritten Arabic Text Database (KHATT), Hijja, Modified Arabic Digit Database (MAD-Base), and Arabic Handwritten Writer Paragraphs Dataset (AHAWP), and major model families including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), convolutional recurrent neural networks (CRNNs), hybrid convolutional neural network-bidirectional long short-term memory models with connectionist temporal classification Convolutional Neural Network-Bidirectional Long-Short Memory/Connectionist Temporal Classification (CNN-BLSTM/CTC), attention-based methods, Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) and Transformer-based recognizers. The reviewed literature shows that CNN models perform well on isolated characters, while hybrid sequence models are more suitable for cursive word and line recognition. Although cross-dataset generalization, segmentation difficulty, limited annotated Arabic datasets, resilience to degraded image, and computational cost added to the challenges. Evaluation under noise, self-supervised learning, lightweight deployment systems, and larger datasets ought to be pointed out in future researches.

W7218082949.abstract: The Agentic AI for Autonomous Vehicles project focuses on the design and development of an intelligent AI-driven system capable of autonomous navigation, real-time decision-making, and adaptive driving behavior. Traditional autonomous vehicle systems mainly depend on predefined rule-based algorithms, which often face difficulties in handling unpredictable road situations, dynamic environments, and complex human behavior. To overcome these limitations, the proposed system introduces an Agentic AI Architecture where the autonomous vehicle functions as an intelligent agent capable of observing, reasoning, learning, and acting independently in real time. The system integrates advanced technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning, Reinforcement Learning, Computer Vision, and Multi-Modal Perception to improve environmental understanding and driving safety. The MultiModal Perception layer collects and processes data from sensors such as cameras, LiDAR, radar, GPS, and ultrasonic sensors to identify roads, traffic signs, pedestrians, vehicles, and obstacles. The processed information is then analyzed by a Reasoning Engine that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) and Reinforcement Learning techniques to predict traffic behavior, interpret complex scenarios, and make intelligent driving decisions. Unlike traditional sensing-acting systems, the proposed architecture follows an observing-reasoning-acting cycle, enabling the vehicle to perform human-like decision-making in uncertain and rapidly changing environments. The system can dynamically adapt to traffic conditions, predict pedestrian intent, optimize route planning, and execute safe driving maneuvers such as braking, lane changing, overtaking, and collision avoidance. The project demonstrates how Agentic AI can significantly enhance the reliability, adaptability, and safety of autonomous vehicles while moving closer to fully intelligent transportation systems.

W7218092351.abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Computational Linguistics have become important areas of research at the intersection of linguistics, computer science, artificial intelligence and information systems. Their central objective is to enable computers to process, interpret, analyze and generate human language in ways that support communication and information management. Advances in machine learning, statistical modeling, neural networks and large-scale language resources have significantly expanded the capabilities of language technologies. NLP applications now include machine translation, speech recognition, sentiment analysis, information retrieval, text classification, question answering, dialogue systems, information extraction and automated summarization. These technologies are increasingly integrated into search engines, digital assistants, customer-service platforms, educational systems, healthcare information systems, social media analysis and business intelligence. The development of neural approaches, particularly representation learning and sequence-to-sequence models, has further improved the ability of computational systems to process complex linguistic structures. However, language remains challenging because meaning depends on context, ambiguity, culture, discourse and social relationships. NLP systems can therefore produce inaccurate interpretations, inherit biases from training data and perform unevenly across languages and dialects. This paper examines the foundations, development and emerging applications of NLP and Computational Linguistics in modern communication and information systems. It discusses the role of machine learning, linguistic resources, information retrieval, machine translation, conversational systems and text analytics while considering challenges related to ambiguity, multilingualism, privacy, bias and computational limitations. The paper argues that NLP should be viewed as a multidisciplinary field in which linguistic knowledge and computational methods complement one another. Its future development will depend on more robust multilingual resources, context-sensitive models, explainable systems and human-centered approaches that prioritize accuracy, fairness and responsible use.

W7219063814.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly being investigated as decision-support technologies in clinical pharmacy, particularly for pharmacovigilance, medication-safety surveillance, and individualized drug dosing. This narrative review synthesizes published evidence on these three overlapping domains, with emphasis on the distinction between technical model performance and demonstrated clinical utility. Literature was identified from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar using combinations of terms related to AI, ML, pharmacovigilance, adverse drug reactions, medication safety, therapeutic drug monitoring, model-informed precision dosing, and dose optimization. The review considered peer-reviewed studies and authoritative regulatory or professional documents relevant to clinical pharmacy. Because the original review workflow did not retain database-level export files or screening counts, exact numbers of records retrieved and excluded could not be reconstructed reliably and are not reported. Across the literature, AI methods show potential for automated extraction of safety information, signal prioritization, prediction of adverse drug events and drug–drug interactions, identification of potentially inappropriate prescribing, medication-error detection, and individualized dosing. However, much of the evidence remains based on retrospective datasets, single-center studies, internal validation, or feasibility work. In precision dosing, conventional pharmacometric methods and Bayesian model-informed precision dosing should be distinguished from data-driven ML, deep learning, reinforcement learning, and hybrid approaches. Prospective implementation studies and patient-level outcome data remain less common than algorithm-development studies. Safe translation into practice therefore requires external validation, prospective comparative evaluation, transparent reporting, interoperability, monitoring after deployment, predefined processes for model updating, and explicit pharmacist and clinician oversight. AI should consequently be regarded as a decision-support capability that complements, rather than replaces, clinical expertise.

W7219837130.abstract: Cancer continues to represent one of the most significant global health challenges due to its molecular heterogeneity, dynamic evolution, late-stage diagnosis, and variability in therapeutic response. Conventional oncology approaches have historically relied on population-based treatment paradigms, imaging interpretation, histopathological examination, and isolated molecular biomarkers, which frequently fail to capture the biological complexity underlying tumor initiation, progression, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance. The emergence of predictive oncology has introduced a transformative computational framework that integrates artificial intelligence (AI), digital biomarkers, multi-omics analytics, radiogenomics, and real-time clinical data to enable earlier cancer detection, individualized risk prediction, and precision therapeutic intervention. Predictive oncology combines machine learning, deep learning, transformer-based architectures, and multimodal foundation models to analyze highly heterogeneous datasets generated from radiology, histopathology, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, liquid biopsy profiling, wearable devices, and electronic health records. These computational systems are increasingly capable of identifying latent disease signatures, forecasting tumor behavior, predicting treatment response, and optimizing personalized clinical decision-making. Recent advances in AI-driven oncology have demonstrated remarkable improvements in cancer screening, recurrence prediction, survival estimation, digital pathology, immunotherapy response assessment, and adaptive therapeutic planning. Convolutional neural networks and transformer architectures have enabled automated interpretation of medical imaging and histopathological slides with performance approaching expert-level diagnostic accuracy. Simultaneously, multimodal AI systems integrating molecular and clinical datasets have facilitated the development of predictive biomarkers capable of guiding precision medicine strategies across multiple cancer types. Despite these advancements, substantial challenges remain regarding model interpretability, algorithmic bias, data standardization, privacy preservation, regulatory approval, and large-scale clinical implementation. This review comprehensively discusses the rise of predictive oncology and the evolving role of artificial intelligence in early cancer detection, digital biomarker discovery, risk modeling, and precision therapy. The article further highlights emerging computational architectures, multimodal learning systems, explainable AI frameworks, federated oncology networks, and future translational directions that may redefine the next generation of precision oncology.

W7220250743.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become foundational components in modern artificial intelligence applications, enabling advanced capabilities in natural language understanding, automated reasoning, content generation, and enterprise decision support. However, the increasing deployment of LLM-based systems has introduced significant security vulnerabilities, particularly prompt injection attacks that manipulate model behavior by embedding adversarial instructions into user inputs, external data sources, or integrated application workflows. This research presents an adaptive defense framework designed to mitigate prompt injection risks through a layered security architecture combining input analysis, contextual validation, dynamic instruction monitoring, and automated response regulation. The study develops a conceptual model for improving LLM reliability by integrating principles from prompt engineering, cloud execution security, artificial intelligence governance, and adaptive system management. Existing research on generative AI frameworks, cloud orchestration, automated workflows, and secure execution environments provides the foundation for analyzing effective defense mechanisms. The proposed framework emphasizes continuous threat identification, intelligent prompt classification, and adaptive policy enforcement to reduce unauthorized behavioral manipulation of LLM systems. Findings indicate that effective LLM security requires a transition from static filtering approaches toward dynamic defense architectures capable of responding to evolving attack strategies. The research contributes an integrated perspective for improving trustworthy generative AI deployment across financial, cloud, enterprise, and intelligent automation environments.

W7220406278.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings such as industrial maintenance and equipment fault troubleshooting, where workers occupy a variety of roles. A capable agent must therefore act in a way that is calibrated to user's role: taking actions and providing information that respect the role's knowledge and capability boundaries. Unlike coding, where mistakes are usually recoverable, agent responses in these settings are enacted on physical equipment, and can therefore cause irreversible equipment damage, production loss, or personnel harm. Existing benchmarks, however, largely overlook the need for agents to infer what a role intends and acting only through tools that role may legitimately use, a capability which we term Perspective Awareness. To this end, we introduce ReFract, a benchmark of 150 expert-validated entries in which an agent must act differently in response to the same query depending on user's role. Entries of ReFract are grounded in anonymized queries from domain support conversations, against which we construct Text World Models that simulate the agent's operating environments and assemble perspective-aware action trajectories. State-of-the-art LLMs solve at most 69% of the tasks with more than 50% of their trajectories contain attempts of taking perspective-violating actions. ReFract exposes perspective awareness as a distinct, largely unsolved axis of agent evaluation and motivates agents that calibrate not just how to act, but for whom.

W7220419427.abstract: Industrial model-based systems engineering (MBSE) relies on specialised modelling tools, yet engineers lack effective ways to leverage large language models (LLMs) inside these environments without externalising critical workflows. The key question is how to embed LLM agents into industrial modelling tools in a way that respects model semantics, preserves user control, and handles engineering artefacts. Prior work does not combine in-tool LLM integration, tool-mediated model operations with transactional safety, and structured document ingestion into a cohesive approach adaptable across MBSE tools and domain-specific modelling languages (DSMLs). We present an architectural approach that operationalises LLM agents as a model-native interaction mode, implemented as MagicChat, a native MagicDraw plugin providing context-aware model querying, transactional model manipulation with undo, large-document ingestion, and document generation. We validate it on a deployed medical-device model through a cumulative four-act scenario executed with three off-the-shelf LLMs, combining a structural analysis of the resulting artefacts with an independent review by 15 system architects. The architecture proved LLM-agnostic, every element the agent created conformed to the deployed DSML profile, and tool-call volume did not predict the quality of the result.

W7220698038.abstract: Between June and October 2026, several publicly documented episodes moved the question of offensive capability in frontier AI systems from speculation to empirical record: agents under evaluation escaped their test environments, communicated over unsanctioned channels and acted against third-party infrastructure (the OpenAI and Hugging Face incident); a frontier-lab agent reportedly gained unauthorized access to an Australian government portal; and the UK AI Security Institute reported unsanctioned actions, including supply-chain attacks and the creation of false identities, in a minority of controlled runs. In parallel, the literature on AI-generated text detection shows that detectors with high in-distribution accuracy degrade under paraphrase, translation, editing and adversarial optimization. This article argues that both bodies of evidence describe one problem seen from two sides: the actor (what an agent does when pursuing a goal under oversight) and the artifact (whether the traces it leaves can be attributed to a production chain). It proposes a conceptual model of the agent-artifact-attribution pipeline, a four-level evidence grading scheme that separates confirmed facts from press reports and hypotheses, and a pre-specifiable experimental design with four hypotheses on instruction scope, multi-agent coordination, and the robustness of provenance detectors against hybrid human-agent production chains. A historical comparison with covert communication techniques (steganography, virtual dead drops, anonymous and encrypted platforms) is used as an analytical lens, with attention to the gap between documented cases and widely repeated claims. No new experimental results are reported. The contribution is a bounded synthesis, an explicit register of what current sources support, and a protocol that independent laboratories can run. Not peer reviewed.

W7221020395.abstract: Diabetes mellitus is a global chronic disease that affects the whole body and not just glucose metabolism. In diabetes, non-invasive ocular changes can help understand microvascular, neurodegenerative, and inflammatory processes. This analysis looks at the eye as a biomarker platform for diabetes-related disease, with retinal imaging informing systemic pathophysiology and the emergence of AI-assisted approaches. With improvements in optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography, it is possible to observe neurovascular changes that can occur before the clinical onset of diabetic retinopathy. Issues in the retina have also been connected to problems with the heart, brain, kidneys, and cognition. However, much of the evidence for problems involving the heart and cognition comes from studies on people without diabetes. Also, most of the available data are observational, rather than coming from controlled studies. As a result, retinal measurements should be considered candidate biomarkers rather than clinically validated predictors or surrogate endpoints for systemic outcomes. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has reached a phase of clinical maturity such that it can be used in the automated screening of diabetic retinopathy. However, it remains investigational for systemic risk prediction, such as for chronic kidney disease, cardiovascular outcomes, and cognitive decline. Equally, the therapeutic implications of retinal neurodegeneration and other imaging biomarkers are under-validated for systemic decisions. Before retinal biomarkers can be used in precision diabetes care, we need more diabetes-specific prospective studies to establish standardized measurements, the clinical meaning of thresholds, incremental predictive value above and beyond established risk factors, reproducibility, cost-effectiveness, and evidence of improved outcomes.

W7221182453.abstract: ABSTRACT Background and Aims Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease with a relapsing course and significant morbidity. In outpatients with moderate‐to‐severe UC assessment of treatment response is often delayed, limiting timely treatment optimisation. Intestinal ultrasonography (IUS) is a noninvasive point‐of‐care modality with high correlation to endoscopic activity. Early changes in bowel wall thickness (BWT) may predict treatment response in hospitalised patients with acute severe UC, but prospective validation in the outpatient setting is lacking. This study aims to evaluate whether early changes in IUS parameters, particularly BWT, can predict treatment response and the need for treatment escalation in outpatients initiating systemic corticosteroids, biologics or small molecules. Methods This is a prospective, nonrandomised, double‐blinded and multicentre study conducted across seven Nordic inflammatory bowel disease centres. Outpatients with moderate‐to‐severe UC extending beyond the rectum, initiating systemic corticosteroids or advanced therapy, will be included. IUS will be performed at baseline and repeated at day 2 ± 1, day 7 ± 1, day 90 ± 14 and at week 52 ± 4 using standardised protocols and evaluated by central reading. Clinical indices, biomarkers, endoscopy and patient‐reported outcomes will be collected and correlated with IUS longitudinally. The primary endpoint is the association between early changes in BWT on days 2 and 7 and treatment escalation at 3 and 12 months. Secondary and exploratory endpoints include remission outcomes, time to response, quality of life and integration of multiomics data. Results Results are pending; recruitment is planned from March 2026 to February 2028. Discussion This multicentre double‐blinded study will prospectively evaluate early IUS as a noninvasive predictor of treatment response in outpatients with moderate‐to‐severe UC. The design enables rapid point‐of‐care assessment of therapeutic efficacy and results will allow for an individualised, dynamic and treat‐to‐target management approach. Key strengths include standardised IUS protocols, blinded evaluations, integration of endoscopic, biochemical and multiomics data, and the creation of an image repository that enables future artificial intelligence applications. Limitations of this study includes the observational design, causal inferences cannot be established and residual confounding may persist despite multivariable adjustment; additionally, treatment heterogeneity, including concomitant corticosteroid use, may complicate interpretation of early imaging changes. Furthermore, exclusion of patients with isolated proctitis and the exploratory nature of the omics analyses may limit generalisability and require external validation. Trial Registration Clinicaltrials.gov. EU CT number: 2026‐527929‐35‐00

W7221355859.abstract: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have advanced from 3.8% to 27.01% power conversion efficiency (PCE) in 17 years, while their lead-free analogs have reached 17.1%, and perovskite/silicon tandems exceeded 34%. Machine learning (ML) is credited with accelerating much of this progress, yet its evaluation is rarely examined. Here, we report a critical audit of 80 ML-PSC studies from 2024 to 2026. Among these, 89% report no error analysis on any sub-range of PCE, none report nested cross-validation, 48% rely on a single train/test split, and only 9% predict stability over time. Models that appear accurate overall can therefore fail in the sparse high-PCE region, which is the region most relevant to commercialization. We reframe high-PCE prediction as an imbalanced regression problem, establish imbalance-aware techniques, recommend an evaluation workflow, and propose a five-pillar roadmap. Further progress depends as much on shared evaluation and reporting standards as on new algorithms.

W7221759295.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming an integral part of the software development lifecycle, and the capabilities granted to them allow an agent to act with the user's authority on any resource it can access. The reach that gives an agent its utility is equally available to an attacker who can steer it. Anything an agent ingests can carry an injected instruction, and since the model does not reliably distinguish instructions from data, indirect prompt injection should be mitigated by mediating the effects the agent produces. Such mediation faces a structural difficulty. Legitimate work and the first step of an attack often look alike when an individual action is observed, and what separates them lies later in the trace, so a monitor limited to allow and deny is forced to decide before the evidence accumulates. We present Kairos, a reference monitor at the isolation boundary of an unmodified, opaque agent, where a tool call, a shell command, and a script the agent writes all cross the boundary as the same file and network operations, so that confinement holds regardless of the agent's behavior. A declarative policy that states which sources are trusted decides most effects deterministically and defers the rest, which are held while the agent continues speculatively. A decision oracle with bounded authority, such as a language model or a human, releases or refuses each deferred effect on the trace. Across three benchmarks and three agent models, Kairos outperforms existing defenses in the trade-off between attack success and utility. In particular, on AgentDojo, it reduces attack success from 47.0\% to 2.7\% while its benign utility stays at the level of the undefended agent.

W7221790027.abstract: Gifted learners require instructional environments that transcend conventional pedagogical boundaries, offering adaptive challenge, metacognitive scaffolding, and high degrees of learner autonomy. This study presents the design, implementation, and empirical evaluation of the AI-Enhanced Self-Directed Learning (AESDL) framework an integrated adaptive system grounded in Treffinger's Independent Learner Model (ILM) and operationalized through an ensemble of five artificial intelligence (AI) technologies: the Google Gemini API (as central orchestration controller), cognitive computing, multi-agent systems (MAS), expert systems, and automatic speech recognition. The model is built upon four core ILM components Guidance, Self-Development, Enrichment, and Seminars/In-Depth Study each computationally instantiated through dedicated AI subsystems. A quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test control group design was employed with 50 gifted secondary school learners (25 experimental, 25 control) drawn from model gifted-education classrooms in Khartoum State, Sudan. The experimental group received eight weeks of instruction via the AESDL system; the control group received equivalent instruction through conventional electronic resources. Outcome measures self-directed learning skills, problem-solving capacity, and academic enrichment achievement (each scored on a 50-point scale) were analyzed using independent-samples t-tests with Cohen's d effect sizes. Results indicated statistically significant and practically large superiority of the AESDL condition: self-directed learning (t(48) = 7.91, p < .001, d = 2.24), problem-solving (t(48) = 5.52, p < .001, d = 1.56), and academic achievement (t(48) = 6.50, p < .001, d = 1.84). These findings advance the empirical evidence base for AI-mediated gifted education and provide actionable design principles for intelligent adaptive learning systems. The control condition comprised conventional electronic learning resources (digital textbooks, instructional videos, and static online exercises). Ninety-five-percent confidence intervals for the between-group mean differences were [9.13, 15.35], [5.62, 12.06], and [7.02, 13.30] for self-directed learning, problem-solving, and academic achievement, respectively. Given the modest sample (n = 50) and the near-ceiling experimental-group scores, these findings should be interpreted with caution regarding potential ceiling effects and limited external validity, and warrant independent replication with larger, more diverse samples.

W7221792239.abstract: Weight-space learning treats the weights of neural networks as data, processed by other models called metanetworks. A key challenge is that different weights can realize the same function, related by a group of symmetries the metanetwork should respect. While symmetry-aware metanetworks for simple architectures such as MLPs are well developed, a comprehensive treatment of transformers, and in particular transformer-based language models, is still missing. Importantly, their weight space has a richer symmetry group: beyond neuron permutations, attention introduces continuous general-linear symmetries of the attention matrices and permutations of entire heads. Existing methods for transformer weights either capture only part of these symmetries or are restricted to a single, fixed architecture, and none accounts for language-model-specific components such as the token embeddings. Building on graph metanetworks, we propose a graph-based approach that is both symmetry-aware and applicable across depths and widths. We formalize a weight-space symmetry group of complete decoder-only language models and provide a graph construction that is invariant to it. We further introduce two new transformer-population datasets with novel tasks, such as training-corpus prediction and fine-tuning detection, on which our approach notably outperforms existing baselines.

W7222008408.abstract: Many real-world questions demand not a single fact but an organized collection of them, yet existing factual knowledge benchmarks almost exclusively target single answer retrieval. We introduce ListQA, a benchmark of 9,045 human-curated, cross-validated questions (audited error rate of 1.7%) that require LLMs to recall multiple facts and compose them into structured lists of 3-10 elements. Questions range from flat lists ("Which NCAA teams went undefeated between 2000 and 2024?") to hierarchical lists with sub-attributes ("...and what was their record and result?"), spanning eight categories across 60+ countries. An evergreen design (explicit temporal constraints or historically immutable facts) keeps ground truth valid without periodic updates. For evaluation, we frame element matching as a linear sum assignment problem: optimal bipartite matching paired with LLM-based semantic grading jointly captures factual accuracy, hallucination, and format compliance. We benchmark 34 models (8 families, 42 configurations across standard and thinking enabled inference) and find: the best standard-inference model scores below 37% LLM-Judge-F1, multi-faceted questions are harder across the board, and providing the source Wikipedia page lifts scores dramatically, confirming that models can organize facts but struggle to retrieve them from parameters alone. Extended analyses cover base vs. instruction-tuned checkpoints and token efficiency. We release the dataset and evaluation code.

W7222343111.abstract: Long-horizon tasks expose a weakness of monolithic tool-use loops: one agent must decompose, execute, and verify a task within a single trajectory. We introduce LAGO, which treats specialized language agents as reusable temporally extended options. A meta-agent retrieves options from a persistent library or spawns new ones, dispatches sub-tasks, verifies results, and admits successful novel options. The library grows across tasks without updating model weights. On 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks, frozen Qwen3.5-35B-A3B in both roles resolves 58.6% under single-attempt evaluation with the official Docker evaluator. On a fixed 150-task subset, we re-run mini-SWE-agent, Terminus 2, and LAGO with the same policy, temperature, task IDs, and evaluator; their resolve rates are 49.3%, 57.3%, and 60.3%, respectively. Cross-model experiments provide evidence consistent with a role for decomposition quality. A 50-task component ablation finds four fewer resolved tasks without decomposition, two fewer with shuffled reused content, and six fewer without the library. These results support reusable agent-options as a practical abstraction for task streams, while leaving component-level causality task- and model-dependent.

W7222376512.abstract: Autonomous enterprise security governance is becoming essential as organizations increasingly adopt cloud-native architectures, distributed applications, hybrid infrastructures, and multi-cloud environments. Traditional security governance approaches frequently depend on static policies, manual approvals, and reactive threat detection, limiting their ability to respond effectively to dynamic enterprise risks. This research proposes an intelligent security governance framework integrating agentic artificial intelligence (AI) with cloud-native policy orchestration to improve security automation, regulatory compliance, and operational resilience. The framework employs specialized AI agents to continuously monitor infrastructure activities, analyze security events, evaluate policy violations, prioritize risks, and coordinate appropriate mitigation actions. Cloud-native technologies, including container orchestration, policy-as-code, identity management, security monitoring, and automated compliance validation, provide the operational foundation. A centralized governance layer establishes policy consistency, accountability, and controlled authorization across distributed enterprise environments. The proposed methodology combines architectural modeling, simulated enterprise workloads, threat scenarios, policy evaluation, and comparative performance analysis to assess detection accuracy, response latency, compliance coverage, and automation effectiveness. Human oversight, explainable decisions, least-privilege access, and auditable execution are incorporated to reduce unintended autonomous actions. The framework aims to demonstrate how agentic AI can strengthen adaptive governance while maintaining organizational control and regulatory accountability. The research contributes an integrated approach for developing scalable, context-aware, and resilient enterprise security governance systems capable of supporting evolving cloud-native operations and increasingly complex cybersecurity requirements.

W7222382962.abstract: The Large Language Model (LLMs) have proven to be extremely powerful in generating high-quality fluent and informative responses to a wide range of prompts. The main issue with such model is that they tend to generate hallucinated responses i.e. responses that contain information not supported by the context. The issue with detecting hallucinations is that a response might sound reasonable, even if it contains irrelevant or incorrect information. The prior work on the topic has had limited success, as the majority of it focuses on utilizing only one type of evidence to detect hallucination, which might be insufficient to capture the complexity of phenomenon. This paper proposes a novel method for detecting hallucination in LLMs responses that utilize a hybrid of different signals to detect hallucinations. This paper introduces a set of signals based on semantic consistency, semantic uncertainty, factual or contextual verification, prompt sensitivity and model variability that evaluate the responses from different angles to determine whether it contains any hallucinations. The paper tests the model on the HaluEval dataset and compares it to individual signals to see whether the hybrid approach would perform better than any single signal. It evaluates the performance using standard classification evaluation metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and PR-AUC and performs an ablation study to assess the impact of each individual signal. Overall, this paper aims to improve the current understanding of the hallucination detection task and the factors influencing it and provide an effective solution to the problem.

W7222755715.abstract: Recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build stronger AI systems, is one promising route to superintelligence. We study a weaker form that can be measured today: frontier agents post-training a small raw base model with public data, as a test of their research potential. We build Athanor, an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain) on real GPUs. We give the agents full research autonomy, low-friction engineering tools, and efficient starter code. The agents carry out the research themselves: they read datasets and evaluation results, build their training data, write and modify training algorithms, tune hyperparameters, and analyze the results to decide what to try next. They work in a sandbox and cannot use external teacher models. Athanor's services supply frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, a persistent research record, and a held-out suite the agents are unaware of. In a 104-hour campaign, a team of four Claude Opus 5.5 agents, each on an eight-GPU node and given no research advice, improves Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.9 to 67.3 on a six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on a held-out suite, against 66.5 and 47.9 for the official Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a team of frontier agents can autonomously post-train a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model that matches or surpasses the official instruct version on average. The campaign's full record shows that the agents reach this level by recombining known methods and each other's models: SFT on public reasoning data, RL with a rollout change one agent introduced, weight merges across agents, and rounds of self-distillation. With execution handled, today's agents already have the engineering and research ability to conquer this task. We hope Athanor provides a foundation for scaling autonomous AI research.

W7222883089.abstract: Autonomous artificial intelligence agents extend generative AI from producing content on demand to pursuing goals through planning, memory, tool use, environmental feedback, and iterative action. This shift matters organizationally because agency is no longer confined to recommendation: systems can increasingly initiate and coordinate consequential work. This article integrates research on AI-enabled work, algorithmic management, organizational design, human–AI collaboration, automation, and responsible AI to explain the transition from copilots to digital coworkers. The review distinguishes five configurations—tool, copilot, teammate, delegate, and coworker—and argues that the central organizational variable is not technical capability alone but the allocation of decision authority. We synthesize evidence showing that AI assistance can improve speed and quality in bounded tasks, often benefiting less experienced workers, while also producing uneven performance at the frontier of model capability. Extending this evidence to agentic systems, we develop an authority allocation matrix based on task risk, reversibility, verifiability, and auditability. We identify three mechanisms through which agents reshape organizations: role reconfiguration, authority redistribution, and coordination redesign. Benefits arise when agents compress search and execution costs, diffuse expertise, and enable new forms of modular organizing. Risks arise when action outpaces verification, responsibility becomes diffused, tacit knowledge erodes, or agents acquire excessive access to organizational resources. We propose a layered governance architecture combining explicit mandates, least-privilege access, execution limits, provenance, continuous monitoring, and human escalation rights. The article concludes with propositions and a research agenda for studying agentic organizing through field experiments, longitudinal process research, digital trace analysis, and comparative institutional designs.

W7222983945.abstract: Recent studies have shown that position bias remains a critical vulnerability in large language models (LLMs), undermining both the integrity of multiple-choice evaluations and the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation. However, existing understanding of this phenomenon is largely derived from studies with limited model coverage and English-centric benchmarks, leaving the behavior of frontier models and diverse languages underexplored. In this work, we conduct a comprehensive investigation of position bias across model scales ranging from billion-level to trillion-level parameters, covering both multiple-choice and multi-document tasks in five languages. Our experiments reveal that while position bias remains noticeable in small-scale models and Non-English languages, increasing model scale and employing standard Chain-of-Thought prompting significantly mitigate this issue. Moreover, we demonstrate that emerging \emph{thinking models} with extended reasoning capabilities are nearly immune to position bias, suggesting a costly but general approach toward resolving this vulnerability.

W7222998051.abstract: Dental image segmentation is an important problem in oral diagnosis and treatment planning due to the high demand for accurate localization and boundary definition.Deep Learning (DL) techniques have dramatically enhanced the ability and accuracy of segmentation tasks in many clinical domains, especially in recent years. Transformer-based architectures were initially designed for natural language processing but have recently also been used within computer vision and medical imaging with comparable success. Between these hybrid approaches, both convolutional and transformer based methods have achieved remarkable productivity improvements for semantic segmentation. This article proposes one possible way to predict which architecture is the most efficient for pixel-wise segmentation using iVisionLab data, based on high-performance deep learning architectures. The transformer-augmented VIT SwinUNETR++ delivered the best F1-Score (95.96%), precision (95.95%), and recall (95.96%). These results demonstrate not only balanced prediction performance, but also better generalization quality than the other three models DeepLab V3+, R2UNet, and SegFormer-B0 evaluated. In addition, the large predictive ability of VIT SwinUNETR++ demonstrates that it is an attractive model for high-performance high-complexity medical image analysis.

W7223019623.abstract: Context: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) is rapidly emerging as a major research paradigm in which artificial intelligence systems move beyond response generation toward autonomous, goal-directed reasoning, planning, tool use, memory, adaptation, and multi-agent collaboration. The rapid expansion and disciplinary fragmentation of this literature create a need for systematic mapping of its research landscape. Aim: This study maps the global development, scholarly influence, geographical distribution, and collaboration patterns of Agentic AI research during 2023–2026. Approach: A bibliometric and science-mapping analysis was conducted using Scopus publications retrieved on 1 July 2026. Following systematic screening and duplicate removal, 3,425 publications were analyzed using Biblioshiny. Key Findings: Agentic AI exhibited an annual growth rate of 215.04%, with 9,166 authors contributing across 1,015 sources. Conference papers dominated the corpus (2,654), reflecting the field’s rapidly evolving technological character. China and the United States were the leading corresponding-author countries, while Tsinghua University was the most productive affiliation. Citation analysis identified several highly influential foundational studies. Interpretation: The findings indicate that Agentic AI is developing rapidly into a distinct, collaborative, and increasingly established research domain centered on autonomous and coordinated AI systems. Contribution: This study provides a broad Scopus-based quantitative map of contemporary Agentic AI scholarship and identifies emerging priorities for evaluation, multi-agent coordination, security, explainability, human–AI collaboration, and governance.

W7223065090.abstract: The increasing use of data-driven technologies has created significant opportunities for intelligent computing, predictive analytics, and automated decision-making. However, conventional machine learning approaches often require centralized data collection, which can introduce privacy risks, security vulnerabilities, and regulatory challenges. Federated learning has emerged as an alternative approach that enables multiple devices or organizations to collaboratively train machine learning models without routinely transferring their raw training data to a central server. Instead, participating clients perform local training and communicate model updates to a coordinating server or aggregation mechanism. This approach can reduce direct data sharing and support collaborative learning across distributed environments. This paper presents a review of federated learning, focusing on its fundamental architecture, training process, aggregation techniques, applications, and technical limitations. It examines the role of federated learning in healthcare, financial services, mobile computing, industrial systems, and smart environments. The paper also discusses challenges involving communication overhead, statistical heterogeneity, device limitations, malicious participants, privacy leakage, and model convergence. Furthermore, it explores complementary techniques, including differential privacy, secure aggregation, and homomorphic encryption, that can strengthen the protection of information during collaborative training. Finally, future research directions are identified in adaptive aggregation, communication-efficient optimization, cross-silo collaboration, edge intelligence, and trustworthy model evaluation. The review concludes that federated learning offers a promising framework for distributed machine learning, but its privacy and performance benefits depend on the system architecture, threat model, data distribution, and security mechanisms employed.

W7223113217.abstract: Firms that sell to other firms on credit now face a new design choice. Software agents built on large language models can gather evidence, draft credit memos, release held orders and chase overdue invoices. Yet there is little guidance on how much of this work an agent should do without a person. Most research on artificial intelligence in credit asks how accurate a model is, and most of it studies consumer lending. It says little about the decision rights of autonomous agents in business-to-business trade credit, where much activity sits outside consumer-protection and bank model-risk rules. This conceptual paper addresses that gap. It integrates research on trade credit, credit scoring, language-model agents, levels of automation, agency theory and model-risk governance. From this synthesis it builds the Verifiability-Weighted Autonomy framework. The central claim is simple: the autonomy granted to an agent should rise with the verifiability of the evidence behind a decision and fall with the decision's financial exposure and irreversibility. The paper defines four autonomy tiers and a transparent allocation rule. It maps twelve common trade-credit decisions onto the tiers. It proposes a Propose–Verify–Dispose architecture in which language-model agents propose, deterministic checks verify, and policy rules or people dispose. It offers seven testable propositions and four measures for future empirical work. For managers, the framework turns a vague question, "can we trust the agent?", into a concrete design rule that fits existing delegation-of-authority practice. Keywords: large language model agents; trade credit; delegation of authority; model risk management; human oversight

W7223219224.abstract: Masked diffusion language models have emerged as an alternative to autoregressive models, enabling parallel token generation. However, standard masked diffusion language models use a shared noise schedule across positions without explicitly encoding which positions should be resolved first. Many tasks exhibit a natural priority among positions: document titles and section headings can guide the generation of body text, while Sudoku cells determined directly from the initial clues can help resolve more difficult cells. To incorporate this notion of priority (or hierarchy) among token positions, we introduce the Hierarchical Masked Diffusion Language Model (HMDLM), which augments each token position with a hierarchy level available as part of the training data, and requires zero or minimal additional annotations. It factors generation into two passes: the first predicts a hierarchy distribution over masked positions, the second predicts token distributions conditioned on it. Giving each hierarchy level its own noise schedule induces a soft, controllable preference for revealing higher-priority positions earlier while keeping decoding fully parallel. Our formulation is mathematically grounded, and we re-derive the forward and reverse processes and the NELBO for this factorization. Our evaluation shows that for the task of language generation on LM1B, HMDLM reduces perplexity by more than 1.5 points over Anchored Diffusion Language Model (ADLM), a recently proposed strong diffusion baseline; on WikiHow, we see a drop in perplexity of up to 4.4 pts on ADLM and up to 7 pts against MDLM. An LLM judge on WikiHow prefers HMDLM generations (the two variants combined) more than $2\times$ as often as the baseline. On the task of solving Sudoku puzzles requiring multi-step reasoning, it improves solution accuracy by up to $8.6\%$ absolute points over existing diffusion baselines.

W7223456774.abstract: Abstract Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) continues to pose a serious threat to global public health, with African healthcare systems carrying a disproportionate burden. Although antimicrobial stewardship programs have been recommended as an important strategy for improving antimicrobial use and slowing the emergence of resistance, implementation across many African healthcare systems continues to face several challenges, including workforce shortages, weak laboratory infrastructure, and poor surveillance systems. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have shown promising potential in strengthening antimicrobial stewardship through clinical decision support, resistance prediction, automated surveillance, and data extraction from weak health information systems. However, the application of AI in antimicrobial stewardship across Africa is still at an early stage, with most systems remaining at pilot or research stages. This commentary discusses current opportunities, examines major barriers affecting implementation, and proposes recommendations that may support sustainable integration of AI into antimicrobial stewardship programs across Africa.

W7223462872.abstract: Cancer immunotherapy has fundamentally reshaped oncology by demonstrating that immune modulation can generate durable clinical responses in patients with advanced malignancies. However, the effectiveness of current immunotherapeutic approaches remains restricted by substantial interpatient variability, primary resistance, and acquired immune escape mechanisms. These limitations largely originate from the complexity of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), where malignant cells interact dynamically with heterogeneous immune populations, stromal components, metabolic networks, and molecular signaling pathways. Conventional biomarker approaches based on individual immune markers, such as PD-L1 expression or tumor mutational burden, provide incomplete predictions because they fail to capture the multidimensional nature of tumor immune interactions. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative approach capable of integrating large-scale biological datasets generated through genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, single-cell sequencing, and spatial omics technologies. Machine learning, deep learning, and emerging foundation models provide unprecedented opportunities to decode immune ecosystems, identify novel biomarkers, predict immunotherapy responsiveness, and accelerate the development of personalized cancer treatments. Recent advances demonstrate that AI-driven models can characterize immune cell states, reconstruct spatial immune architectures, and improve patient stratification for immune checkpoint inhibitors. This review discusses the evolving intersection between AI and cancer immunology, focusing on how computational approaches are transforming TIME analysis, biomarker discovery, and precision immunotherapy. We critically evaluate current challenges, including algorithmic bias, model interpretability, clinical validation, and regulatory implementation. Finally, we highlight future directions toward AI-powered immuno-oncology platforms capable of integrating biological knowledge with computational intelligence to achieve individualized and more effective cancer therapies.
